key_terms.meaning: Moves every point by a fixed offset: x′ = x + tₓ, y′ = y + t_y; it is not a linear map, so it is written as a matrix only with homogeneous coordinates.
Turns a point by angle θ counter-clockwise: x′ = x cos θ − y sin θ, y′ = x sin θ + y cos θ.
Multiplies coordinates by factors sₓ and s_y: x′ = sₓ·x, y′ = s_y·y; factors below 1 shrink, above 1 enlarge, negatives flip.
Slides one axis along another: with shear factor k, x′ = x + k·y, y′ = y; the amount of slide grows with distance from the axis.
A 2D point (x, y) written as (x, y, 1); the extra third value lets translation be expressed as a 3×3 matrix multiply.
A single matrix that maps the column vector (x, y, 1)ᵀ to (x′, y′, 1)ᵀ; its first two rows hold the linear part, its third column holds the translation.
The product of several transformation matrices, in the order the transforms are applied, that does the whole sequence in one multiply.
If A is applied first and B second, the combined matrix is B·A, not A·B; matrix order is the reverse of application order.
Rotating about a point P is done as: translate P to the origin, rotate, translate back, i.e. T(P)·R(θ)·T(−P).
The 3D form: the point (x, y, z) becomes (x, y, z, 1), and every 3D affine transform is a 4×4 matrix with a 3×3 linear block and a translation column.
Coordinates are transformed so the chosen axis becomes one of X, Y or Z, the simple 3D rotation is applied, then coordinates are transformed back.
The rectangle in world coordinates that the user has chosen to show, for example x from x_wmin to x_wmax and y from y_wmin to y_wmax.
The rectangle, in device or screen coordinates, where the window contents are finally drawn; it sets the picture's position and size on the screen.
A scale plus a shift on each axis: x_v = x_vmin + (x − x_wmin)·(x_vmax − x_vmin)/(x_wmax − x_wmin), and the same form for y.
A line through P₀ = (x₀, y₀) with direction d = (dx, dy) is P(t) = P₀ + t·d; clipping means finding the range of t, usually 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, that lies inside the window.
Four bits per endpoint recording whether the point is above, below, right of or left of the window; two zero codes mean the line is fully inside.
Solves the four inequalities p·t ≤ q for t and keeps the overlap of the resulting intervals; it uses only division by the line direction components.
Clips the polygon's edge list against one window boundary at a time, producing a new, shorter edge list after each boundary.
For the left boundary, a point is inside when x ≥ xmin; each edge is handled by comparing its two endpoints, giving four cases per boundary.
The coordinate frame attached to the camera: eye position, view direction, and up vector define it, and the scene is transformed into it.
Projectors are parallel, so objects keep their size however far they are; the projection plane simply drops one coordinate.
Projectors pass through a centre of projection, so distant objects look smaller; the projected point is scaled by 1/z.

takeaways: Every 2D transform is a rule (x, y) → (x′, y′); translation and rotation and scaling are affine, so they keep straight lines straight and parallel lines parallel.
Adding a third coordinate of 1 to a point makes all four 2D transforms 3×3 matrix multiplies, and their products are the only tool needed to build complex motion.
Matrix order matters: the transform written last in the product is the one applied first to the point.
In 3D the same four transforms act on (x, y, z) and become 4×4 matrices; a rotation about any line is done by moving that line onto an axis and back.
Window-to-viewport mapping is nothing but independent scale-and-shift on x and y, and it is what turns a designed world into pixels on the screen.
Line clipping reduces to finding the parameter range of t that satisfies all four window inequalities, and Cohen–Sutherland does this cheaply with 4-bit outcodes.
Wang's or Liang–Barsky style parametric tests beat the older endpoint tests when many long lines cross the window, because each boundary is tested once.
Polygon clipping is edge-list processing: consider each boundary in turn, keep the inside parts, and close the polygon with the boundary segment where the edge leaves and re-enters.
A 3D picture needs two things before it appears: a camera frame (viewing coordinates) and a projection, parallel for scale drawings and perspective for realistic views.
bank_note: Long answers here usually ask for a derivation followed by a worked numeric example, so keep the matrix form beside the algorithm steps.

bank.q: Explain homogeneous coordinates. Why is a translation impossible as a 2×2 matrix but easy as a 3×3 matrix?
outline: A 2×2 matrix applied to (x, y) can only produce combinations of x and y; a constant offset cannot appear.
Take the point (x, y) as (x, y, 1) and use a 3×3 matrix with the offset in the third column.
Show translation, rotation and scaling matrices side by side.
State that the third row is (0 0 1), so the third coordinate stays 1 for points.
Mention the general form (hx, hy, h) for h ≠ 0 and its use in perspective.

bank.q: Write the 2D rotation and scaling matrices and derive the matrix for rotation by θ about an arbitrary pivot point (x_p, y_p).
outline: Rotation matrix rows: (cos θ, −sin θ, 0) and (sin θ, cos θ, 0).
Scaling matrix with sₓ and s_y on the diagonal.
Pivot rotation equals T(x_p, y_p)·R(θ)·T(−x_p, −y_p).
Multiply the three matrices and show the result's third column.
Note that a point at the pivot does not move.

bank.q: Give the 4×4 matrices for 3D translation, scaling and rotation about the Z axis, and explain how rotation about an arbitrary axis is carried out.
outline: 4×4 form with (x, y, z, 1) and last row (0 0 0 1).
Translation column in the fourth column; scale on the main diagonal.
Z-axis rotation keeps the z row and column at identity.
Arbitrary axis: translate the axis to the origin, rotate it onto X/Y/Z, apply the simple rotation, then invert both steps.
State the full product M = T⁻¹·R⁻¹·R(θ)·R·T.

bank.q: Define window and viewport and derive the window-to-viewport mapping equations.
outline: Window defined in world coordinates, viewport in device coordinates.
Relative position is preserved, so (x − x_wmin)/(x_wmax − x_wmin) = (x_v − x_vmin)/(x_vmax − x_vmin).
Rearrange to get the scale factor and the shift.
Same derivation for y.
Small windows mapped to big viewports zoom in; unequal aspect ratios stretch the picture.

bank.q: Describe the Cohen–Sutherland line clipping algorithm: outcode bits, the four cases, and how the intersection is computed.
outline: Four bits: top, bottom, right, left.
Both codes 0 → accept; logical AND ≠ 0 → reject.
Otherwise choose an outside endpoint and clip against one boundary.
Intersection from the parametric line equation, for example y = y₁ + m(x − xmin).
Repeat until accept or reject; state that the clipped endpoint gets a new outcode.

bank.q: A triangle with vertices A(1, 1), B(3, 1), C(2, 3) is scaled by 2 in both axes about the point (2, 2) and then rotated by 90° about the origin. Find the single composite matrix and the new vertices.
outline: Build R for θ = 90° with cos 90° = 0 and sin 90° = 1.
Composite M = R·S, since scaling is applied first.
Multiply M by each vertex in homogeneous form.
List the transformed vertices and check one by hand.

bank.q: A window has corners (0, 0) and (4, 4). A viewport has corners (1, 1) and (3, 3). Find the mapping and locate the image of the window point (2, 1).
outline: Scale factors 2/4 = 0.5 on both axes.
Substitute (2, 1) to get (2, 1.5).
Check that the window centre (2, 2) lands at the viewport centre (2, 2).
Mention that coordinates are then rounded to integers by the rasterizer.

bank.q: Use Cohen–Sutherland to clip the line from (−2, 3) to (5, −1) against the window xmin = 0, ymin = 0, xmax = 4, ymax = 4. Show every step.
outline: Outcodes: P₁ has the left bit set; P₂ has the bottom and right bits set.
AND is 0, so the line must be clipped, not rejected.
Clip P₁ against the left boundary to get (0, 2.14).
Clip the right or bottom boundary next, giving the exit point.
Final segment and its two intersection points.

bank.q: Use the Liang–Barsky algorithm to clip a line against a rectangular window. State the p and q values for all four boundaries and show how t_start and t_end are updated.
outline: Direction dx = x₂ − x₁, dy = y₂ − y₁.
Left/right: p = −dx, q = x₁ − xmin; p = dx, q = xmax − x₁.
Bottom/top: p = −dy, q = y₁ − ymin; p = dy, q = ymax − y₁.
p = 0 means the line is parallel to that boundary: reject if q < 0.
For p < 0 update t_start = max(t_start, q/p); for p > 0 update t_end = min(t_end, q/p).
Reject if t_start > t_end, else substitute t back into the line equation.

bank.q: Clip the polygon with vertices (1, 1), (5, 1), (5, 4), (1, 4) against the window x ≥ 2 using Sutherland–Hodgman. Show the vertex list produced at each stage.
outline: Treat the window as four boundaries and clip left first.
For each edge compare both endpoints with x ≥ xmin and apply the four cases: in-in, in-out, out-in, out-out.
Insert intersection points where edges cross x = 2.
The first pass changes the square into a smaller square with x from 2 to 5.
Remaining boundaries leave the list unchanged; note the repeated closing vertex.

bank.q: Compare Cohen–Sutherland and Liang–Barsky line clipping. Which is faster in which situation, and why?
outline: Cohen–Sutherland repeats the whole clip step after each boundary, so intersections may be computed many times.
Liang–Barsky tests each boundary once and needs no floating-point division unless a crossing exists.
Cohen–Sutherland is simple and quick for lines fully inside or fully outside.
Liang–Barsky wins for long lines crossing the window with many boundaries.
Both are O(1) per line but with different constants; very few lines are truly clipped in typical scenes.

bank.q: Explain the full 2D viewing pipeline from world coordinates to screen pixels, and say at which stage clipping happens and why there.
outline: World coordinates → normalised device coordinates by the window-to-viewport map.
Clip against the window or clip rectangle before rasterisation.
Reasons: fewer pixels to fill, avoids overflow of integer screen coordinates, avoids drawing outside the visible area.
Then rasterise primitives, fill, and write to the frame buffer.
Note that clipping in normalised coordinates and in device coordinates is equivalent if the map is affine.

bank.q: Compare parallel and perspective projections. Describe how a camera model fixes the view, and evaluate which projection suits a technical drawing and which suits a first-person game.
outline: Camera defined by eye point, look-at point and up vector; viewing coordinates built from these.
Parallel projection keeps sizes; plan and elevation views are parallel.
Perspective divides by depth, giving foreshortening and vanishing points.
Technical drawing and CAD use parallel because measurements stay true.
Games use perspective because depth cues look natural.
Mention the view volume and the need to clip in 3D before projection.

bank.q: A graphics program applies the same rotation to 10 000 vertices. Compare storing each transform separately against pre-multiplying into one composite matrix, and explain the role of the homogeneous 3×3 matrix in this choice.
outline: Separate application costs one matrix-vector multiply per transform per vertex.
One composite matrix costs one multiply per vertex, plus a fixed matrix product.
The matrix product is done once at setup, so cost drops from k multiplies to 1 per vertex.
Point out that the composite stays a 3×3 affine matrix, so it is still one multiply and one add per coordinate.
Warn about floating-point error and about the reverse order of multiplication.

bank.q: A scene contains many polygons crossing a window boundary. Discuss what goes wrong if polygons are clipped edge by edge without Sutherland–Hodgman, and how a one-boundary-at-a-time pass avoids it.
outline: Clipping each edge independently leaves the polygon open; it has no new closing edge.
Sutherland–Hodgman keeps the inside portion of each edge and adds the boundary segment between exit and entry points.
After each boundary the result is still a closed polygon, so the next boundary can be applied to it.
Note that the method assumes a convex clip window and produces extra edges on concave polygons.

glossary.def: A map of the form x′ = a·x + b·y + c, y′ = d·x + e·y + f; lines stay lines and parallels stay parallel.
A transform made only of rotation and translation, so lengths and angles do not change.
The fixed point about which a scaling or rotation is performed.
A transform that flips a point across a line or plane, achieved with scale factors of −1 on one axis.
A representation that carries an extra coordinate, allowing translation and perspective to be written as matrix multiplies.
Multiplying transform matrices together to obtain one matrix that performs the whole sequence.
Removing the parts of a primitive that lie outside a given region before it is drawn.
The rectangle, in the coordinate system used for clipping, that limits what is kept.
The case where a primitive lies wholly inside the clip window and needs no further work.
The case where a primitive lies wholly outside one boundary and is discarded at once.
A short bit pattern recording which sides of the clip window a point lies outside of.
A line described by a starting point and a direction vector with a parameter t running along it.
A polygon in which every line segment joining two interior points stays inside the polygon.
A polygon clipper that processes the edge list once per window boundary.
A parametric line clipper that computes the interval of t lying inside all four window boundaries.
The transform that converts world coordinates into the camera's viewing coordinates.
The flat surface onto which a 3D scene is projected to make a 2D picture.
The point from which perspective projectors are drawn; also called the eye or viewpoint.
A parallel projection in which the projector direction is perpendicular to the projection plane.
The effect in a perspective projection where objects farther from the eye appear smaller.
The point on the picture where parallel lines in a scene appear to meet under perspective projection.
An intermediate coordinate system, usually with both axes between 0 and 1, used before mapping to pixels.
The 3D region the camera can see; everything outside it is clipped away.
